Subdomain Takeover Checker

Paste a hostname. This follows its real CNAME chain over public DNS, and when the chain ends at one of 25 known takeover-prone providers, sends one live GET request and checks the response against that specific provider's own "nothing is claimed at this name" page — a confirmed finding, not a guess from DNS alone. See why CNAMEs end up dangling for the common causes and the fix. This tool never attempts to claim, register, or configure anything at any provider — detection and reporting only. Only run this against a hostname you own or are authorised to test.

Run the check

Enter a hostname, then click Check.

Report

CNAME chain

HopHostname

Prefer a CLI, or hit a CORS wall in the browser?

The DNS lookup always completes (Cloudflare's resolver answers CORS-enabled), but most third-party providers don't send permissive CORS headers on their catch-all "not found" page, so the confirming GET request often cannot complete from a browser tab — you'll see the finding reported as unconfirmed rather than confirmed. The CLI has no such restriction and is the one path guaranteed to complete: 

node check.mjs blog.example.com --json

Get check.mjs, lookup.mjs, probe.mjs, fingerprints.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if any hostname is confirmed or unconfirmed-risky, so you can gate a deploy or a DNS-zone review on it.

Common questions

What is a subdomain takeover?

A DNS CNAME record on your domain still points at a third-party service (an S3 bucket, a Heroku app, a GitHub Pages site), but whatever used to be configured there has since been deleted or was never created. Many of those services let anyone claim an unclaimed name on their platform — and once they do, they can serve their own content under your subdomain, complete with your domain's own cookies and any trust your CSP or CORS policy places in it.

How does this tool confirm a takeover risk rather than just guessing from DNS?

It follows the hostname's CNAME chain over real DNS first. If the chain ends at a hostname matching one of 25 known takeover-prone providers, it sends one live GET request to your hostname and checks the response against that specific provider's own "nothing is claimed at this name" page text. Only a match on both — the CNAME target and the live response — is reported as confirmed; a CNAME match with no confirming response is reported separately, as worth a manual look rather than proven. See how this compares to checking with dig by hand.

Does this tool claim the vulnerable name for me, or otherwise fix it?

No. It only detects and reports. Claiming the resource yourself (creating the S3 bucket, the Heroku app, the GitHub Pages repo under the exact name your CNAME expects) is the actual fix in most cases, alongside removing the DNS record if the subdomain is no longer needed at all — see the guide page for the walkthrough.

Is it safe to point this at a hostname?

This tool sends one DNS lookup and, only for a provider match, one ordinary GET request to the hostname you name — the same requests your own browser already makes when you visit it. It never attempts to claim, register, or write anything at any provider. It does not upload the hostname or anything it finds to our servers when run in the browser; every request goes straight from your browser to the DNS resolver and the target. Still, only run this against a hostname you own or are authorised to test.

Does a clean report mean my whole domain has no dangling CNAMEs?

It means the hostnames you checked in this run showed no CNAME risk this tool's 25-provider table could detect. This tool only checks the exact hostnames you give it — it does not enumerate your DNS zone or guess at other subdomains — and it only recognises the providers in its table. See README.md's coverage note for what that does and does not include.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks the hostnames you give it against a table of 25 known takeover-prone providers, with one DNS lookup and (for a match) one GET request each. It never writes, submits, or claims anything, never enumerates your DNS zone, and cannot see a risk from a provider it does not know about. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the domain has no exposure anywhere.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every request goes straight from your browser to the DNS resolver and the hostname you name — never through this site, and never logged or stored by us. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day — no hostnames, no response bodies, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Also worth a pass on your stack: Dotenv Exposure checker and Git Exposure checker cover other static-file exposure classes, Security Headers checker covers another response-evidence class in the same "read what's actually there, name the exact evidence" shape as this tool, and CAA Record checker covers a different DNS-hygiene footgun -- which certificate authority is allowed to issue for your domain, rather than a dangling CNAME.

vs-checking-dig-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the Subdomain Takeover Checker

Subdomain Takeover Checker vs. checking with dig by hand

Running dig CNAME blog.example.com is a real, fast way to see where a hostname points. It is also the method most developers already reach for first, and it genuinely shows you the target.

Checkdig by handThis tool
Seeing the CNAME targetCatches itCatches it
Recognising the target as one of ~25 known takeover-prone providersYou have to already know the pattern (which of dozens of hostnames like *.herokuapp.com, *.s3.amazonaws.com, *.azurewebsites.net actually matter)Matched against a maintained provider table automatically
Following a multi-hop CNAME chain to its real endManual, one dig per hopFollowed automatically, up to 8 hops
Confirming the target is actually unclaimed right now, not just provider-shapedRequires a second manual step: opening the URL and reading the responseOne live GET request, checked against that specific provider's own "unclaimed" fingerprint page
Checking a whole list of hostnames in one run, repeatable in CIManual, one at a timeCLI accepts multiple hostnames and returns a real exit code

When to still just use dig

If you only need to see where one hostname currently points, dig is fine — it's already on your machine and you're already there. The gap this tool closes is recognition and confirmation: knowing which of the target's dozens of possible shapes actually matters, and proving the name is genuinely unclaimed with a live fingerprint match rather than assuming risk from the DNS target's shape alone.

Common questions

What does running dig CNAME by hand actually show you?

dig CNAME blog.example.com shows you the CNAME target — a real, fast way to see where a hostname points. It does not tell you whether that target is one of the roughly two dozen hosting providers known to let an unclaimed name be claimed by anyone, and it does not tell you whether the target is actually unclaimed right now versus in active, legitimate use.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Three ways this scripted check catches and a quick dig lookup misses: (1) recognising which of dozens of possible CNAME target patterns actually belongs to a takeover-prone provider — a hostname like old-app.herokuapp.com means nothing to dig, which just prints the string. (2) Following a multi-hop CNAME chain to its real end rather than stopping at the first hop. (3) Confirming the target is genuinely unclaimed with a live HTTP request checked against that specific provider's own "nothing is claimed at this name" page — a CNAME pointing at a provider is not proof of anything on its own; plenty of CNAMEs to Heroku or S3 are perfectly legitimate and in active use.

Why does this matter for a DNS-zone review, not just a one-time check?

A manual dig is a point-in-time look at one hostname you already thought to check. A decommissioned service, a provider migration, or a sunset campaign page can leave a new dangling record behind at any point. The CLI here returns a real exit code across as many hostnames as you give it in one run, so it can gate a periodic DNS-zone audit the same way a linter gates a deploy.

why-cnames-end-up-dangling.html.text:
← Back to the Subdomain Takeover Checker

Why CNAMEs end up dangling

A dangling CNAME only becomes a takeover risk once someone else claims the name it points at. There are a few common, independent ways the record is left behind in the first place. Fixing one does not fix the others.

1. Decommissioning the resource doesn't touch DNS

Deleting an S3 bucket, a Heroku app, or a GitHub Pages repository is usually a one-click action in that provider's own dashboard — and it does not touch your DNS zone at all. The CNAME record you created when you first set the subdomain up keeps pointing at a name that now belongs to nobody, until someone remembers to remove it separately, in a different system. 

# Wrong: delete the S3 bucket and stop there
aws s3 rb s3://old-marketing-page-bucket --force
# blog.example.com's CNAME still points at old-marketing-page-bucket.s3-website-us-east-1.amazonaws.com

# Right: remove the DNS record in the same change
aws s3 rb s3://old-marketing-page-bucket --force
# then, in your DNS provider: delete the CNAME for blog.example.com

2. It's not on the offboarding checklist

The fix is procedural, not technical: whatever runbook or ticket template your team uses for decommissioning a service, add "remove the DNS record pointing at it" as a required step, in the same place as "revoke the API key" and "delete the database". A resource that still exists is not takeover-prone; the dangling record left behind after it's deleted is.

3. Nobody audits the zone on a recurring basis

A team that migrates providers, retires a marketing campaign's landing page, or sunsets an old product line accumulates dangling records the same way — each individually easy to miss, and each dangling indefinitely until someone claims it, maliciously or otherwise. A recurring pass over your own DNS zone's CNAME records, checked against what's still actually provisioned, catches what any one migration's checklist did not.

If this checker already found a confirmed finding

Two ways to close it, and you usually want one or the other rather than both:

  • Still using it: reclaim the exact name on the provider (recreate the S3 bucket with that name, recreate the Heroku app, re-add the GitHub Pages custom domain) before anyone else can.
  • Not using it anymore: remove the CNAME record from your DNS zone entirely — the subdomain then stops resolving, which is safe, rather than continuing to point at a name someone else could still claim.

Run the Subdomain Takeover Checker again afterward to confirm the fix. Only run it against a hostname you own or are authorised to test.
